The Marxophone is a fretless zither, a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 314.122. Its face carries two octaves of paired melody strings tuned to C major, plus four sets of chord strings: C major, G major, F major and D7. The player usually strums the chords with the left hand while the right hand presses the spring-steel strips so that the little lead hammers at their ends strike the strings; a short press gives a single note, and holding it down produces a mandolin-like tremolo from the paired strings. Its timbre is close to the mandolin and to the various hammered dulcimers, and modern recording artists and film scores use it occasionally, as do alternative rock and alternative country recordings.
馬克索風琴未成為大眾常見樂器，但實際用於錄音室作品、影視配樂與現場演出。它出現在: The Marxophone never became a common instrument, but it is used in studio work, in film and television scores and in live performance. It turns up in rock, alternative country and avant-garde music, and is used in television scores and small live shows. Particular pieces include "Tippecanoe and Tyler Too", "I Am Trying to Break Your Heart" and "Soul Meets Body", showing that its particular timbre has been added to the line-up.
馬克索風琴的擊槌機構由亨利·查爾斯·馬克斯於1912年取得專利，常被誤認為密西根: The Marxophone's hammer mechanism was patented by Henry Charles Marx in 1912, and the instrument is often wrongly said to have been made by the Marxochime Colony of New Troy, Michigan. The patent passed to the company Marx then belonged to, which made the Marxophone and another instrument with a differently shaped body, and merged in 1926. A new company then made it from 1926 to 1931, and two further companies carried it on into the 1950s. It was advertised as easy to learn and sold through salesmen and by mail order. From the late twentieth into the twenty-first century it has appeared occasionally on recordings, entering pop and alternative music.
馬克索風琴的音色明亮而富有穿透力，帶有輕快的金屬質感。其雙旋律弦設計使音域達到兩: The Marxophone's timbre is bright and carrying, with a light metallic quality. Its paired melody strings give a range of two octaves, from middle C to C'', with pitches clearly defined, well suited to melodic lines. The sound comes from metal hammers striking the strings, resonating like a struck instrument, with an immediate response and a quick decay. Its colour falls between the bright sharpness of the mandolin and the warmth of the hammered dulcimer, holding something of both. The four sets of chord strings add rich harmonic layers, so that it can play a melody and accompany itself at once. Altogether it sounds light and expressive, suited to chamber playing and solo settings.
